blocks.x: CSM 177 · Topic 9 of 10

Slides communicate best when text is paired with graphics and multimedia. This topic covers inserting and formatting pictures and SmartArt diagrams, arranging objects precisely on a slide (aligning, distributing, grouping, rotating, stacking), and adding movies and sound to bring a presentation to life.

6alignment options — Left, Center, Right, Top, Middle, Bottom 4stacking commands — Bring to Front, Bring Forward, Send to Back, Send Backward 3sound sources — file on computer, clip organizer, audio CD track
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Insert and modify pictures using the Ribbon, resize and move them correctly, and apply Picture Styles, Picture Shape and Picture Border using the Picture Tools Format tab.
2Insert and modify SmartArt diagrams, choosing an appropriate diagram type (List, Process, Cycle, Hierarchy, Relationship, Matrix, Pyramid) and converting bulleted text into a SmartArt graphic.
3Align, distribute and group objects precisely, understanding the difference between "Align to Slide" and "Align Selected Objects".
4Rotate objects and control stacking order, distinguishing Bring to Front/Send to Back from the one-layer-at-a-time Bring Forward/Send Backward commands.
5Insert, resize and delete movies and sound clips, choosing a playback trigger (Automatically or When Clicked) and using Audio Tools Options for CD tracks.

blocks.x: Key definitions
Multimedia object Any non-text element placed on a slide — a picture, clip art, SmartArt diagram, movie or sound clip — used to communicate graphically rather than through text alone.
Free Rotate handle The green circle that appears above a selected object; dragging it rotates the object freely around its center.

SmartArt graphic A visual diagram built from a layout template (e.g. List, Process, Cycle, Hierarchy, Relationship, Matrix, Pyramid) that PowerPoint can generate from a bulleted list or from scratch via the Insert tab.
Stacking order The front-to-back layering of overlapping objects on a slide. Objects inserted later sit on top of objects inserted earlier, by default.
Grouping Combining two or more selected objects into a single unit so they can be moved, resized or rotated together as one object; the Group command can later be reversed with Ungroup.

sections.title: Inserting a picture from the Ribbon

blocks.x: Graphics on the slide
Pictures and SmartArt diagrams let a slide communicate visually — illustrating a point, showing a process, or replacing a wall of bullet text with a clear graphic.
Inserting a picture from the Ribbon

items: 1On the Insert tab, in the Illustrations group, click the Insert Picture command (sometimes labelled "Pictures").
2In the dialog box that opens, browse to and locate the picture file on your computer or storage device.
3Select the file and click Insert to place the picture on the current slide.

blocks.x: Resizing and moving
Corner sizing handles Dragging a corner handle resizes a picture proportionally — height and width change together, keeping the image from looking stretched or squashed.
Side sizing handles Dragging a side (top, bottom, left or right) handle resizes only one dimension, which distorts the picture's proportions.
Moving a picture Click on the picture and drag it to a new position on the slide. The green circle above the selected picture is the Free Rotate handle — drag it to rotate the picture freely.
Modifying a picture

items: 1Picture Styles — apply a ready-made frame/shadow/border combination to the picture. Click the More dropdown arrow in the Picture Styles gallery to see the full set, with live preview as you point to each style before clicking to apply it.
2Picture Shape — changes the picture's outline from a rectangle to another shape (oval, star, arrow, etc.), cropping it into that shape.
3Picture Border — adds an outline around the picture; choose a border color and a line weight (thickness).
4Cropping — trims unwanted edges from a picture so only the desired portion shows.
5Compressing — reduces picture file size to keep the presentation file smaller.
6Resetting a picture — undoes all formatting changes made to the picture, restoring its original appearance.
7Contrast and Recolor — Contrast adjusts the difference between light and dark areas; Recolor applies a color tint or converts the picture to grayscale/black-and-white/washout, etc.

blocks.x: Inserting and modifying SmartArt

items: 1On the Insert tab, click the SmartArt command.
2In the gallery, select a diagram type and layout that fits the content you want to show.
3Click OK to insert the SmartArt graphic, then type or paste text into its shapes.

blocks.x:
Converting a bulleted list to SmartArt
An existing bulleted text placeholder can be selected and converted directly into a SmartArt diagram (right-click the placeholder, or use "Convert to SmartArt" on the Home tab), turning plain bullet points into a visual graphic without retyping the text.
Types of SmartArt graphics

c: Steps in a task or workflow, in sequential order
A continuous, repeating sequence of stages
An organization chart or decision-tree relationship
Connections between two or more ideas, such as overlapping or converging concepts
How parts relate to a whole, in quadrants
Proportional or hierarchical relationships, built from the base upward

blocks.x: A picture is inserted from a file and edited with the Picture Tools Format tab (Styles, Shape, Border, Crop, Compress, Reset, Contrast, Recolor). A SmartArt graphic is a diagram built from a layout template chosen from the Insert tab's SmartArt gallery, and can also be created by converting an existing bulleted list.
Precise slide layout
When a slide holds several objects, PowerPoint's Align, Distribute and Group commands line them up neatly and let related objects be handled as one unit.
Selecting and aligning multiple objects

items: 1Click and drag a selection box around the objects to select them all at once (or click one object, then Shift-click the others).
2On the Format tab, click the Align command to open the alignment menu.
3Choose an alignment option; the objects snap into position accordingly.

blocks.x: The six alignment options
Align Left / Align Right Lines up the selected objects' left edges (or right edges) along a common vertical line.
Align Center Lines up objects along a common vertical center line (horizontal centering).
Align Top / Align Bottom Lines up the selected objects' top edges (or bottom edges) along a common horizontal line.
Align Middle Lines up objects along a common horizontal center line (vertical centering).
Align to Slide vs Align Selected Objects

Align to Slide Each alignment command positions the selected objects relative to the edges/center of the entire slide — e.g. "Align Center" centers every selected object on the slide's horizontal midpoint.

Align Selected Objects Each alignment command positions the objects relative to each other only — e.g. "Align Center" lines the selected objects up on a shared vertical line based on their own combined bounding area, without reference to the slide as a whole.

Distribute Horizontally / Distribute Vertically Spaces three or more selected objects evenly across the horizontal or vertical dimension. Like the six alignment options, the result differs depending on whether Align to Slide or Align Selected Objects is active — distributing across the whole slide width versus across just the selected objects' own span.
Grouping and ungrouping objects

items: 1Select the multiple objects to combine (selection box or Shift-click).
2On the Format tab, click the Group command, then choose Group from the menu.
3The objects are combined into one unit that can be moved, resized or rotated as a whole.
4To reverse this, select the grouped unit, open the Group command again, and choose Ungroup to split it back into individual objects.

blocks.x: Why group objects? Once grouped, dragging any part of the group moves every object in it together, keeping their relative positions fixed — useful for diagrams built from several shapes, text boxes and pictures that should always move as a set.

Forgetting to check whether Align to Slide or Align Selected Objects is active is the most common cause of unexpected alignment results — the same "Align Center" click can either center objects on the slide or merely line them up with each other, depending on this setting.
Depth and orientation
Beyond position, objects on a slide also have an orientation (rotation) and a front-to-back layering order that controls which object appears on top when objects overlap.
Rotating objects

items: 1Select the object to rotate.
2On the Format tab, click the Rotate command.

3Point to a rotation option (e.g. Rotate Right 90°, Rotate Left 90°, Flip Vertical, Flip Horizontal) to see a live preview before clicking to apply it. The green Free Rotate handle can also be dragged for a custom angle.

blocks.x: How stacking order works

Default stacking order Objects on a slide are layered according to the order in which they were inserted: the first object inserted sits at the back of the stack, and each object inserted afterward is placed on top of the ones before it.
Back (inserted 1st)→ Middle (inserted 2nd)→ Front (inserted 3rd, topmost)
Ordering commands

c: Moves the selected object all the way to the top of the stack, above every other object
Moves the selected object one layer forward (toward the front), past just the next object
Moves the selected object all the way to the bottom of the stack, beneath every other object
Moves the selected object one layer backward (toward the back), past just the next object

blocks.x: "Bring to Front" and "Send to Back" jump an object to the extreme top or bottom of the stack in one click. "Bring Forward" and "Send Backward" move an object only one position at a time — useful when several objects overlap and only a small adjustment to the layering is needed.

sections.title: Inserting a movie from a file

blocks.x: Multimedia
Movies and sound clips add motion and audio to a presentation. PowerPoint lets you insert them from a file, a placeholder icon, a clip organizer, or an audio CD, and choose how playback is triggered.
Inserting a movie from a file

items: 1On the Insert tab, click the Movie dropdown and choose Insert Movie from File.
2In the dialog box, locate and select the movie file.
3Choose the playback trigger: Automatically (plays as soon as the slide appears) or When Clicked (plays only when the user clicks it during the slide show).
4Once inserted, the Movie Tools Options tab and the Picture Tools Format tab appear for further formatting.

blocks.x: Resizing a movie A movie object is resized the same way as a picture — using its corner and side sizing handles (corner = proportional, side = distorts proportions).

Inserting via a content placeholder A slide layout with a content placeholder shows a small set of icons in its center; clicking the Insert Media Clip icon opens the movie/media browser directly, without needing the Insert tab.
Deleting a media clip Click to select the movie or sound object, then press the Delete key to remove it from the slide.
Inserting sound

items: 1Sound can be inserted from a file on the computer, from the clip organizer (a library of pre-installed sound clips), or from an audio CD's tracks.
2As with movies, choose whether the sound plays Automatically when the slide loads or When Clicked during the presentation.

blocks.x: Audio Tools Options (CD tracks)

c: Plays the selected track so it can be checked before running the slide show
Sets playback level to Low, Medium, High, or Mute
Edited to set exactly which track (and which point in time within it) playback should start and stop at
Switches the playback trigger between Automatically and When Clicked
Hides the sound/CD icon so it is not visible while the slide show is running
Repeats the track continuously until the slide show moves on or the sound is manually stopped

blocks.x: Both movies and sound clips share the same two playback-trigger choices: Automatically (starts on its own when the slide appears) and When Clicked (waits for the presenter or viewer to click the object during the show).
